notes.maama: Also a polite way to address any older woman.
notes.taata: Also a polite way to address an older man.
notes.rafiki: The same word for one friend or many.
notes.wange: For people: mama wangu, rafiki wangu.
notes.wako: For people: baba wako, your father.
notes.wake: His or her: Swahili doesn’t mark gender.
notes.huyu: For a person: Huyu ni nani? Who is this?
notes.mzee: A respectful word for an older person, often used as a title: Mzee Juma.
notes.caayi: Usually milky and sweet, often spiced with ginger or cardamom.
notes.ugali: Stiff maize porridge, eaten with the hands with stew or greens. In Uganda it’s called posho.
notes.nsoma: Kusoma is both to read and to study.

guidebook.intro: Family in East Africa is wide: cousins are brothers and sisters, any older woman can be mama, and a grandmother’s word carries weight.

tips.title: My, your, his, her
body: “My” comes after the noun. For people it is usually **wangu**, **wako**, **wake**: **rafiki wangu** (my friend), **mwalimu wako** (your teacher), **mjukuu wake** (his or her grandchild).

With close family words (**mama**, **baba**, **kaka**, **dada**, **bibi**, **babu**) many speakers use the **y-** forms instead: **mama yangu**, **baba yako**. You’ll hear both; this course uses **yangu** with family and **wangu** with other people.

tips.title: Nina and sina
body: “To have” is **-na** with a person in front: **nina** (I have), **una** (you have), **ana** (he or she has).
To say you don’t have something, change the start: **sina** (I don’t have), **huna** (you don’t have), **hana** (he or she doesn’t have).

tips.title: People nouns: m- and wa-
body: Swahili sorts nouns into classes, each with its own prefix. Most words for people start with **m-** for one and **wa-** for more: **mtu**, **watu**; **mtoto**, **watoto**; **mwalimu**, **walimu**.
Describing words and numbers copy the prefix: **mtu mzuri** (a good person), **watu wazuri** (good people), **watoto watatu** (three children).

culture.title: Mama and baba for everyone
body: It is polite to call an older woman **mama** and an older man **baba** or **mzee**, even a stranger. Parents are often called after their first child: **Mama Neema** is Neema’s mother.

culture.title: Bibi’s proverbs
body: Grandparents are famous for **methali** (proverbs). You met one already: **Haraka haraka haina baraka**, “hurry, hurry has no blessing”.
